rv.q: It is a penetrating production, lean, charged and fresh with a concentrated central performance: celebrity casting, for a change, more than pays off.
Always baffling, never boring, and completely mad in its own way.
But it’s a show in which you see what they were going for rather than really feel it.
It’s a fascinating experiment, one that’s beautiful, but ultimately impenetrable.
And, as with the Old Vic’s Oedipus — which features another Hollywood star, Rami Malek, in the title role — it proves only fitfully successful.
Nevertheless, the words are glimmers in a murky evening.
It is so self-consciously stylised, so artful and so devoid of any genuine sense of humanity in extremis that it’s more likely to provoke a yawn or a weary eye roll than pity or terror.
It’s a “No” from me to this capitalised approach.
Yet this West End debut at the Duke of York’s Theatre for the Californian star of Captain Marvel and Lessons in Chemistry is an unrewarding experiment.
Larson, with buzz-cut hair and a punk T-shirt, goes in for a one-note grump of a performance, unhelped by a verbose version by the poet Anne Carson.
But the production, full of strangeness and insight, feels half-baked, as if all its elements haven’t quite had time to gel.
Her voice is deliberately flat, which often jars, particularly when she is reunited with her brother and her reaction is borderline emotionless.
Unfortunately, Fish’s revival is overladen with misfiring gimmicks, while it neglects key elements of the drama.
The effect is of a formal exercise that hasn't tapped a reservoir of feeling.
So why is Daniel Fish’s Elektra such a droning dud?
If you enjoy innovative and original theatre, then this bold, exhilarating take on Elektra is well worth your time.
Fish's 75-minute production is concise, well-acted and slick, but prioritises style over substance.
But repeating “No” soon becomes a repetitive tick and a somewhat shallow idea.
Sadly, Elektra falls into that category though I take no joy in saying that.

cn.t: Larson's fierce performance anchors Fish's polarizing, experimental production that divides critics with its stark, punk-inflected aesthetic. While some praise its haunting feminist edge, many find it a soulless, over-directed misfire prioritizing style over substance.

vr.q: It is neither the most thrilling nor the most satisfying evening that I have spent at the theater so far this year but it's also definitely not the worst.
